title: Periodontitis & the BPE
blurb: How gum disease destroys the ligament and bone, the signs to spot, and how to record the Basic Periodontal Examination (codes 0–4 and *).
question: The dentist walks a probe around each tooth and calls out one number for each sixth of the mouth: "Upper right 3, upper anterior 2, upper left 4 star…". The patient asks what the numbers mean and whether his gums can go back to how they were. How do you record the scores, and what would you tell him?

teach.h: Periodontitis: when the damage goes deeper
teach.body: Periodontitis is chronic inflammation that has spread from the gums into the supporting tissues: the periodontal ligament, cementum and alveolar bone. The body's own inflammatory response to plaque bacteria breaks these tissues down. The gum detaches from the root, a true pocket forms, and bone is lost. Unlike gingivitis, this loss of attachment is irreversible: treatment can stop it progressing, but lost bone and ligament don't simply grow back. It is often painless, so many patients don't know they have it.

steps.label: Gingivitis
steps.sub: Plaque and calculus inflame the gums; REVERSIBLE

steps.label: Periodontitis
steps.sub: Attachment and bone lost; true pockets; IRREVERSIBLE

teach.caption: Not everyone with gingivitis goes on to periodontitis. Persistent plaque plus a susceptible patient (for example a smoker or someone with poorly controlled diabetes) drives it forward.
The bone level has dropped, a true pocket has formed beside the root, and calculus sits below the gum margin.

Left: healthy gums. Middle: heavy calculus with red, bleeding gum margins (gingivitis). Right: the gums have receded, exposing roots with dark subgingival deposits, and a gap has opened between the central incisors: periodontitis.

teach.body: Periodontitis shows as bleeding on probing, true pocketing, gingival recession with exposed roots, loss of the gum between teeth (dark 'black triangles'), drifting or spacing of teeth, and mobility as bone is lost. Patients may notice a bad taste or breath, or pus. Recession exposes root dentine, so cold sensitivity and root caries become more likely. Radiographs show the bone loss. Many patients feel no pain until the disease is advanced.

teach.h: Measuring it: pockets and the BPE
teach.body: Pocket depth is measured from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket. The BPE is a quick screen using a WHO probe, which has a 0.5 mm ball end and a black band from 3.5 to 5.5 mm. With a light force of 20–25 g, the dentist walks the probe round every tooth in each of the six sextants (each needs at least two teeth) and calls out the highest code found. You record one score per sextant. The dentist may then stage (I–IV) and grade (A–C) the disease under the 2017 classification.

bands.label: Healthy
bands.sub: Pockets under 3.5 mm, black band fully visible, no bleeding. No treatment.

bands.label: Bleeding on probing
bands.sub: Black band fully visible. Oral hygiene instruction (OHI).

bands.label: Calculus or overhang
bands.sub: Black band fully visible. OHI, remove calculus and plaque-retentive factors.

bands.label: Pocket 3.5–5.5 mm
bands.sub: Black band partly visible. As code 2, plus 6-point charting of that sextant after treatment.

bands.label: Pocket over 5.5 mm
bands.sub: Black band disappears. Full-mouth 6-point charting before and after treatment; consider referral.

bands.label: Furcation involvement
bands.sub: Added to the code, e.g. 3* or 4*.

teach.caption: A box of six: upper right, upper anterior, upper left on top; lower right, lower anterior, lower left underneath. Record the highest code in each sextant, exactly as called.

teach.text: Pocket depth runs from the GINGIVAL MARGIN to the base of the pocket (attachment loss is measured from the CEJ). And * is never a score on its own: it's added to the number, as in 3* or 4*, to show furcation involvement.

items: Health → gingivitis → periodontitis; only gingivitis is reversible.
Periodontitis destroys periodontal ligament and alveolar bone: true pockets, recession, mobility.
Recession exposes root dentine, causing cold sensitivity and root caries risk.
BPE: WHO probe, 20–25 g, six sextants, highest code per sextant.
Codes: 0 healthy, 1 bleeding, 2 calculus/overhang, 3 pocket 3.5–5.5 mm, 4 over 5.5 mm, * furcation.
Treatment: OHI, risk-factor control, professional plaque and calculus removal below the gum, then supportive maintenance.
Bleeding on probing means plaque control needs reinforcing.

summary: You can now explain how periodontitis destroys the supporting tissues and why it is irreversible, list its signs, compare it with gingivitis, describe how pocket depth is measured and how a BPE is carried out, and record and interpret BPE codes 0–4 and *.

A.q: A patient asks how gum disease develops. Which sequence is correct?
A.why: Plaque first causes gingivitis; in susceptible patients it progresses to periodontitis with loss of attachment.

whyNot.0: Gingivitis develops from health, not the other way round.
whyNot.3: Periodontitis can't reverse back to health; lost attachment doesn't regrow.

A.q: What does a BPE code 3 indicate?
A.why: Code 3 means the deepest pocket in the sextant is 3.5–5.5 mm, with the black band partly visible.

whyNot.0: Bleeding with no pocketing or calculus is code 1.
whyNot.1: Calculus or an overhang with shallow pockets is code 2.
whyNot.3: Pockets over 5.5 mm (black band disappears) are code 4.

A.q: Which structures are destroyed in periodontitis?
options: Enamel and dentine at the gum line
Pulp tissue and the apical foramen
A.why: Periodontitis breaks down the supporting tissues: the periodontal ligament and the alveolar bone.

whyNot.0: Enamel and dentine are destroyed by caries or tooth wear, not periodontitis.
whyNot.1: The pulp is affected by caries, not periodontitis.
whyNot.2: Inflammation of the gingival margin alone is gingivitis.

B.q: From where to where is a periodontal pocket depth measured?
options: CEJ to the base of the pocket
B.why: Probing (pocket) depth is measured from the gingival margin down to the base of the pocket.

whyNot.1: Measuring from the CEJ gives loss of attachment, not pocket depth.
whyNot.2: The incisal edge isn't a periodontal landmark.
whyNot.3: The apex can't be reached with a probe; it's seen on radiographs.

B.q: During a BPE, the black band of the probe disappears completely into a pocket in the lower left sextant. Which code is recorded?
B.why: If the black band disappears, the pocket is over 5.5 mm, which is code 4.

whyNot.0: Code 1 is bleeding with the black band fully visible.
whyNot.1: Code 2 is calculus or an overhang with the black band fully visible.
whyNot.2: Code 3 is when the black band is only partly visible (3.5–5.5 mm).

B.q: A patient with periodontitis says a lower incisor feels loose. What is the main cause?
options: Loss of supporting bone and ligament
B.why: As periodontal ligament and alveolar bone are destroyed, the tooth loses support and becomes mobile.

whyNot.0: Caries damages tooth tissue but doesn't loosen the tooth in its socket.
whyNot.1: Erosion wears the tooth surface; it doesn't cause mobility.

C.q: Why might a patient with periodontitis complain of cold sensitivity on several teeth?
options: Calculus conducts cold to the pulp
Pockets fill up with cold saliva
Bone loss exposes the pulp chamber
C.why: Gingival recession exposes root dentine, whose tubules transmit cold to the pulp.

whyNot.0: Calculus doesn't conduct cold to the pulp.
whyNot.2: Saliva in pockets isn't the cause of sensitivity.
whyNot.3: Bone loss doesn't expose the pulp chamber.

C.q: Several sites bleed while a 6-point pocket chart is being recorded. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Record it and take no further action
C.why: Bleeding on probing shows active inflammation from plaque, so oral hygiene and plaque removal need reinforcing.

whyNot.0: Brushing less leaves more plaque and more bleeding.
whyNot.1: Interdental cleaning is essential for removing plaque between teeth.
whyNot.3: Bleeding must be recorded and acted on, not ignored.

C.q: What does an asterisk (*) next to a BPE score show?
C.why: The * is added to the code (for example 3*) when the probe enters a furcation between the roots of a multi-rooted tooth.

whyNot.2: An overhang is a code 2 finding.
whyNot.3: A sextant with fewer than two teeth isn't scored; the BSP example grid shows it with a dash.

reteach.title: A fence post in soil
reteach.question: Picture a fence post set in soil. What happens if weeds grow at its base, and what happens if the soil washes away?

blocks.body: Weeds round the base of a post are like gingivitis: untidy, but pull them out and the post is fine. Periodontitis is the soil washing away down the side of the post. A gap opens beside it (a pocket), the post starts to wobble (mobility), and if enough soil goes, the post falls (tooth loss). You can stop more soil washing away, but the lost soil doesn't come back by itself. The BPE is how the dentist measures how deep that gap goes.

blocks.caption: Bone and gum have dropped down the root: the 'soil' has gone.

explain.body: In periodontitis the periodontal ligament and bone are destroyed and the gum detaches from the root, forming a true pocket. Treatment can halt it, but lost attachment doesn't simply regrow.

test.q: What is the key difference between gingivitis and periodontitis?
test.why: Periodontitis involves irreversible loss of attachment and bone; gingivitis affects only the gums.

whyNot.2: Inflammation of the gums only is gingivitis.
whyNot.3: Bone loss is a feature of periodontitis.

explain.body: True pockets, recession, black triangles between teeth, drifting, mobility, bleeding, pus and bad breath. It is often painless until late.

explain.caption: Gingival recession, dark subgingival calculus, and a gap between the lower central incisors where gum and bone support have been lost.

test.q: Which of these is a sign of periodontitis rather than gingivitis?
test.why: Mobility comes from loss of bone and ligament support, which only happens in periodontitis.

whyNot.0: Bleeding happens in both gingivitis and periodontitis.
whyNot.1: Red margins are seen in both.
whyNot.3: Plaque is present in both; it is the cause.

explain.body: WHO probe (0.5 mm ball, black band 3.5–5.5 mm), light force of 20–25 g, walked round every tooth in each sextant. The position of the black band gives the code.

test.q: What force should be used when probing during a BPE?
options: As hard as the patient tolerates
No pressure; the probe just rests
A light force of about 20–25 g
test.why: BSP guidance is a light probing force of 20–25 g, which gives accurate readings without damaging the tissue.

whyNot.0: 100 g is far too heavy and would push through healthy tissue.
whyNot.1: Probing to tolerance is inaccurate and uncomfortable.
whyNot.2: Some force is needed to reach the base of the pocket.

explain.body: The mouth is split into six sextants. For each, record the single highest code the dentist calls, in a box of six. A furcation is shown by adding * to the number.

test.q: How is the BPE score for each sextant recorded?
options: The highest score found in it
The average of all its scores
The score of the first tooth
The lowest score found in it
test.why: Only the highest (worst) code found in each sextant is recorded.

whyNot.1: Averaging would hide the worst site.
whyNot.2: Every tooth is probed; the first tooth isn't special.
whyNot.3: Recording the lowest would miss disease.
